extracted.intended_audience: students, policymakers, bankers, and economists interested in monetary and capital theory
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and analytical principles about fixed vs circulating capital, the distinction between money and real revenue, and the effects of banking and paper money on industry and national revenue. Covers what counts as neat revenue, how savings or substitutions (e.g., paper for specie) affect productive capacity, and which uses of foreign exchange are beneficial or harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed capital excluded from neat revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense for erecting and supporting fixed capital (machines, buildings, instruments of trade) is part of gross revenue but must be deducted from the neat revenue of the society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed capital's purpose is to increase productive powers of labour; though profitable over time, its erection and maintenance require a portion of annual produce and therefore are deductions from neat revenue. Compare to repairs on a private estate: necessary repairs maintain gross/neat rent, while avoidable savings in these expenses increase neat revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention and evaluation of fixed capital investment
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed capital is intended to increase the productive powers of labour (enable same labour to produce more); improvements that reduce costs without diminishing productive power are advantageous to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investments in machinery/buildings that reduce the expense of performing work (e.g., cheaper, simpler machinery achieving same output) free materials and labour for other productive uses and therefore augment the annual produce and neat revenue. Example: an undertaker reducing machinery maintenance cost will employ saved funds to buy more materials and hire more workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components of circulating capital and their effect on revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulating capital consists of money, provisions, materials, and finished work; of these, provisions, materials, and finished work may contribute to neat revenue, but money (specie) is distinct and its maintenance alone can diminish neat revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three parts (provisions, materials, finished work) are regularly withdrawn and become part of fixed capital or stock reserved for consumption; only the money component of circulating capital can reduce neat revenue because money itself is not consumed but merely circulates value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue measured by purchasing power, not metal pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: A person's or a society's real revenue consists in the consumable goods (the money's worth, purchasing power) they can obtain, not in the mere metal pieces of money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between counting 'money' as metal pieces versus counting the value of goods purchasable with that money (e.g., a weekly guinea's value is what it can buy). For society, circulating metal pieces are far less than aggregate pensions because the same pieces circulate among many people; revenue therefore equals successive purchasing power, not the physical coins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of paper for specie can increase productive funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing gold and silver money with paper (bank notes) can reduce the costly instrument of commerce and free specie for productive uses, thereby increasing the funds available to maintain industry and augmenting annual produce and neat revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When bank notes serve the purposes of money by confidence in payment, much less specie is needed in circulation; the freed specie can be used abroad to buy materials or supply new trade (carrying trade), or domestically to buy materials/tools/provisions that employ more labour. Example: Scottish banking increased trade/industry by allowing circulation with less gold/silver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on the practicable quantity of circulating paper
rubrics_metrics.description: The total amount of paper money that can circulate easily in a country cannot exceed the value of the gold and silver which it replaces (or which would be required if there were no paper money); excess paper issues will overflow the domestic channel and provoke redemption demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If paper exceeds the sum needed to transact domestic exchanges (given the lowest denomination), the surplus cannot be used at home nor sent abroad and will return to banks for redemption. Banks must reserve specie to meet demands; excessive issuance results in immediate returns and pressure on bank coffers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of bank-issued promissory notes and cash accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Banks issue promissory notes and grant cash accounts (credit lines secured by sureties), allowing notes to circulate as money and enabling merchants to carry on larger trades with less idle specie held on hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Banks gain by discounting bills and lending via promissory notes; merchants with bank credit avoid keeping large sums idle for occasional payments, so with the same stock they maintain larger warehouses and employ more workers. Scottish cash accounts (easy repayment, piece-meal) encouraged the acceptance of bank notes and expanded trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of how exported specie is employed
rubrics_metrics.description: When specie forced abroad by banking operations is used to purchase foreign goods, the impact on national neat revenue depends on what is purchased: buying goods for carrying trade or goods that enable productive industry adds to neat revenue; buying luxuries for idle consumption is harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If specie finances carrying trade or purchases materials/tools/provisions that employ labour and reproduce their value, gross and neat revenue increase. If specie buys luxury consumables for idle people that do not augment production, it promotes prodigality and harms the society. Majority behaviour and class patterns influence likely outcomes; historically, specie sent abroad tended to be used for productive purchases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Savings in maintenance that do not reduce productive power increase neat revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Any saving in the expense of erecting or supporting fixed capital (or of collecting/supporting money) that does not diminish the productive powers of labour is an improvement of neat revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to improved machinery that costs less to maintain: savings free funds to be reallocated into circulating capital (materials, wages) and thereby increase annual produce. Similarly, cheaper means of circulating money (paper vs specie) lower maintenance expense and can augment neat revenue if productive capabilities remain unchanged.
